content: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is a musculoskeletal condition characterized by pain in the front and behind the kneecap. Various non-surgical treatments are available for this condition, including the use of knee orthoses such as braces, sleeves, straps, or bandages. These devices are worn over the knee and are believed to alleviate pain. They can be used alone or alongside other treatments like exercise or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of knee orthoses in treating PFPS. The authors conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries up to May 2015 to identify relevant randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials. The primary outcomes assessed were knee pain and function. Five trials involving 368 participants with PFPS were included in the review. Participants were recruited from health clinics in three trials, while the other two trials involved military recruits undergoing training. None of the trials included elite or professional athletes, although military training involves rigorous physical activity. All five trials were deemed to have a high risk of bias, particularly due to challenges in blinding participants and care providers. The quality of evidence for all reported outcomes was rated as very low using the GRADE approach, indicating significant uncertainty about the results. The trials examined three types of comparisons: knee orthoses combined with exercises versus exercises alone, one type of orthosis versus another, and knee orthoses versus exercises. None of the trials investigated the mode of orthosis use, such as whether the device was worn continuously or only during physical activity. The trials varied in design, with two trials having two groups, two trials having three groups, and one trial having four groups. All trials included a no treatment control group, with all participants receiving exercise therapy either through a military training program or a home-based exercise program. The evidence suggested no clinically significant differences in short-term knee pain (2 to 12 weeks) between groups using knee orthoses and those not using them. Pain was measured using a visual analogue scale (0 to 10 points, with higher scores indicating worse pain), and the mean difference was -0.46 in favor of knee orthoses (95% confidence interval: -1.16 to 0.24; p = 0.19; 234 participants, 3 trials). Similarly, no meaningful differences were observed in knee function (183 participants, 2 trials). None of the trials reported on quality of life, resource use, or participant satisfaction. Two trials assessed the impact on sporting or occupational participation, but the data were limited. One trial did not provide treatment group-specific data on resumption of sports, while the other reported only on military training abandonment due to knee pain, with both cases involving participants allocated to knee orthoses. Adverse events were reported in one trial involving 59 participants (84 affected knees). In this trial, 16 knees (36% of 44 knees) in the knee orthoses groups (both using knee sleeves) experienced discomfort or skin abrasion. Three trials compared different types of knee orthoses, including a knee brace versus a knee sleeve (63 participants), a patella strap versus a knee sleeve (31 participants), and a knee sleeve with a patellar ring versus a knee sleeve alone (44 knees). None of these trials found significant differences in pain between the orthoses. One trial found no meaningful difference in function between a knee brace and a knee sleeve. Adverse effects were more common in participants using knee sleeves with a patellar ring compared to those using knee sleeves alone. One trial compared a knee orthosis (knee brace) with exercise alone (66 participants). The evidence from this trial suggested no clinically significant differences in pain or knee function between the two groups. This trial did not report on quality of life, impact on sporting or occupational participation, resource use, participant satisfaction, or complications. In conclusion, this review found insufficient evidence to support the use of knee orthoses for treating PFPS. The available evidence, which is of very low quality, suggests that knee orthoses do not significantly reduce knee pain or improve knee function in the short term (less than three months) in adults undergoing exercise therapy for PFPS. High-quality, clinically relevant research is needed to better understand the role of commonly available knee orthoses in managing this condition.
